name: Moving the goalposts
statement: Moving the goalposts is raising the standard of proof after it has been met, so that a conclusion survives evidence that was supposed to settle it.
meaning: The move has three beats. A standard is stated or implied, evidence arrives that meets it, and the standard is then replaced with a harder one. What makes it a fallacy is the timing and the reason. The new standard was chosen after the result was known, and chosen because of it. Standards do improve as evidence accumulates, and a test tightened because the old one was shown to be weak is inquiry working properly. The same tightening, applied only to results the arguer dislikes, is the fallacy. A charge of moving the goalposts therefore has to show that the shift tracked the conclusion rather than the quality of the test, and that is a claim about somebody's reasons, which they can deny and usually do. Two neighbouring entries describe different manoeuvres. No true Scotsman narrows the category a claim is about until the counterexample falls outside it, leaving the sentence intact and empty. The motte-and-bailey fallacy changes which claim is being defended, retreating from a bold one to a modest one that shares its wording. Moving the goalposts leaves the claim and the category alone and changes the test they have to pass. The criterion is the part of the three that a laboratory can fix in advance. An experimenter can set a standard, then vary whether meeting it suits the participant, and count what the participant does. What follows is that measurement, not a test of the rhetorical move.

origin.who: George Hardie, as reported in The Scotsman
origin.note: A football metaphor with no coiner and no founding text. The earliest figurative use located is a report in The Scotsman of Saturday 3 May 1924 on a Commons debate about proportional representation. The Labour member for Springburn, George Hardie, is quoted saying that the Liberals, having been beaten, 'not only wanted to change the rules of the game, but wanted to shift the goal posts because they could not play any more'. That passage was read at Pascal Tréguer's Word Histories rather than in the newspaper, because the British Newspaper Archive is paywalled, and the parliamentary occasion could not be confirmed. Hansard's online sittings calendar for 1924 lists no Commons sitting between 15 April and 5 May, and its index page for the Proportional Representation Bill lists debates from 1872 to 1983 with none in 1924. Gary Martin's Phrase Finder gives a first citation 63 years later, Nigel Lawson quoted in the Jamaican Gleaner in September 1987, and says the phrase reached wide British use in the 1980s. Tréguer also found the literal joke behind the figure, in the Forfar Dispatch of 21 February 1946 and 11 March 1948, where 'shift the goalposts' is what a crowd shouts at a team that keeps missing.

evidence: No experimental literature on the named fallacy was found in the searches recorded under limits. The manoeuvre underneath it has three, and none of them uses the name. Peter Ditto and David Lopez put the amount of evidence demanded on a counter. In their first study, 67 female undergraduates at Kent State decided which of two contestants was more intelligent by turning over analogy questions one at a time, believing they would then work with whoever they chose. Seven were dropped, leaving 60, fifteen to a cell. When both contestants were likeable, the number of questions taken did not depend on which way the answer came out, 9.9 against 8.8, F(1, 56) = 1.12, p = .29. When the target was dislikable, participants stopped after 6.6 questions to conclude he was the less intelligent of the two, and took 9.1 to conclude he was the more intelligent, F(1, 56) = 5.99, p < .02. Studies 2 and 3 moved the same question to a fake saliva test for a fictitious enzyme condition, thioamine acetylase. Told that an unchanged yellow strip meant a deficiency, participants took 104.8 seconds on average to accept that the test had finished, against 76.5 seconds for those told the identical strip meant they were healthy, t(45) = 2.60, p < .02, and 13 of 25 retested themselves against 4 of 22. The deficiency group redipped the original strip up to twelve times. In Study 3 the diagnosis was made equally unexpected in both conditions. Those told the condition was unhealthy listed 1.7 recent life irregularities that might have spoiled the test, against 0.5 for those told it was healthy, F(1, 75) = 13.16, p < .01. They also rated the test less accurate, 5.6 against 7.3 on a nine-point scale, F(1, 73) = 11.31, p < .01. Ditto and Lopez read all of this as a difference in how much processing unwelcome information gets, and they set that against Kunda's account, in which different inference rules are reached for directly. The motivated reasoning entry covers that argument and the polarisation literature it grew into. What a separate page adds is the criterion itself. These studies measure the standard a person applies rather than the conclusion they reach, and in the first study every participant in the analysed sample reached the correct conclusion in the end. Michael Norton, Joseph Vandello and John Darley did the same thing to hiring criteria over six studies. Ninety-three male undergraduates ranked five candidates for a construction job, of whom two were live options, one more educated and one more experienced. With no first names attached, 76% picked the more educated candidate. When the more educated candidate was a man, 75% did. When she was a woman, 43% did. The written justifications followed the choice: education was named the more important qualification by 48% and 50% of the first two groups and by 22% of the third, and gender was named by 0%, 8% and 14%. Their second study removed the slack by making 46 participants equate the two candidates themselves, and the selection bias went. The demand for evidence took its place, with the group whose better-educated candidate was a woman wanting to see more resumes, 6.29 against 5.25 on a seven-point scale, F(2, 45) = 2.69, p = .08. That is the closest measure on this page to raising a standard, and it did not reach significance. Their fifth study made 123 participants accountable for their decisions and the reweighting did not shrink, rising from 63% to 76% of participants ranking whichever qualification favoured their chosen candidate above the other, χ²(1, N = 123) = 2.22, p = .14. Their sixth had 72 Princeton students rank eight qualifications before seeing any resumes, and 86% put grade point average above the number of advanced classes. They then selected the black candidate 76% of the time, taking the higher-GPA candidate 84% of the time when he was black and 32% of the time when he was white. The rerankings barely moved, with 74% still calling GPA the more important. The 27 who contradicted their own preranking were no less confident in their decision than those who did not. Eric Uhlmann and Geoffrey Cohen reported three studies of the same shape in 2005. Their abstract, read at Crossref, states that participants 'redefined the criteria for success at the job as requiring the specific credentials that a candidate of the desired gender happened to have', and that 'commitment to hiring criteria prior to disclosure of the applicant's gender eliminated discrimination'. That last clause is what Norton's sixth study contradicts, and the two have not been reconciled here. Neither the abstract nor any source reached gives their sample sizes, so no number is put on those three studies. This literature is small and old. Norton's six studies ran 93, 46, 209, 154, 123 and 72 students, and Ditto's three ran 67, 51 and 93 before exclusions. No repetition of the constructed-criteria or casuistry procedure by anyone was located, preregistered or otherwise, and the searches are named under limits.

replication.headline: Four preregistered studies in the medical-feedback paradigm found no devaluation of the test. Ten preregistered experiments on judgment thresholds found people breaking standards they had set themselves.

study.cite: Araiza, A. M., & Freitas, A. L. (2020). Do people devalue sources of threatening health feedback particularly when its criteria are ambiguous and its consequences enduring? Collabra: Psychology, 6(1), 17. Four preregistered studies, abstract only.

replication.detail: Ashley Araiza and Antonio Freitas preregistered four studies on whether threatening health feedback makes people disparage the instrument that produced it, which is the prediction Ditto's Studies 2 and 3 turn on, and they cite Ditto and Lopez. Their abstract reports that across all studies, contrary to their predictions, there were no significant effects of feedback on participants' ratings of the accuracy of the assessment procedures. Studies 1 to 3 used undergraduates and both unambiguous and ambiguous assessment items; Study 4 varied whether the consequences described were enduring or fleeting. Their full text sits behind a Cloudflare challenge and was not obtained, so no sample size is quoted here, and the abstract was read twice, once as the JATS abstract at Crossref and once through the Semantic Scholar API. On the other side, Nadav Klein and Ed O'Brien report ten preregistered experiments with 5,542 participants on thresholds people set for themselves before judging others, such as promising a reward after three good deeds. People then act after two, or hold out for four, while every behaviour obeys the threshold they set. Which way they go depends on how much support the particular case supplies, with higher support making them quicker to judge and lower support slower. Their abstract also reports initial evidence that violating a preset threshold risks damaging the violator's reputation and relationships. That is the only measurement found of whether the shift costs anything with an audience. Its full text was not obtained either, and its abstract was read twice, at Europe PMC and through the NCBI eutils interface. Neither paper repeats the other's procedure and neither is labelled a replication. The state is mixed because the prediction has been put to preregistered test more than once and the answers disagree, not because one team reran another team's study.

limits: Nothing here is a test of the fallacy as argued about. No experiment was found in which one party shifts a standard and another party is asked to notice, name or judge it. That search covered Europe PMC, Crossref, OpenAlex, the Semantic Scholar citation graph and general web search. Europe PMC holds 95 records containing 'moving the goalposts' and 26 containing 'move the goalposts'; adding 'fallacy' to the first query leaves two, a review of the maternal microbiome and a paper in imaging genomics, both using the phrase in passing. The search for a repeat of the hiring-criteria procedure covered Europe PMC, where 'constructed criteria' returns 53 records of which the only relevant one is Uhlmann and Cohen's own and 'casuistry' with 'social category bias' returns only Norton's own, Crossref, and general web search. Two sweeps were cut short. OpenAlex refused further queries on a daily budget limit, and the Semantic Scholar citation endpoint returned zero citations for Uhlmann and Cohen while Crossref counts 350 works citing it, which is an indexing gap rather than a finding. Only Ditto and Lopez and Norton and colleagues were read as full texts. Uhlmann and Cohen, Araiza and Freitas, and Klein and O'Brien were read as abstracts, so nothing is said here about their methods beyond what those abstracts state. No effect size is quoted for any of the five papers, because none was found in what was read. Three internal discrepancies are worth recording. Ditto and Lopez give Study 2 a final sample of 48 after three exclusions, then report the latency test as t(45) and the retesting chi-square as N = 47. Ditto and Lopez give the no-deficiency decision latency as 76.5 seconds in the text of Study 2 and as 75.5 in Table 1; both readings were confirmed with two independent PDF extractors, and the text figure is the one used above. Norton and colleagues give 32% in the selection paragraph of Study 6 and 31% two paragraphs later for what appears to be the same proportion. The 1924 quotation is at one remove, from Word Histories rather than from The Scotsman, and the Commons sitting it describes is not in Hansard's index for that week. Whether an earlier figurative use exists is unknown; two phrase researchers who looked reached dates 63 years apart.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating any raised standard as the fallacy. Criteria are supposed to get harder when a test is shown to be too easy, and the accusation is empty unless it can point to a reason for the shift other than the result. Norton's sixth study shows what the evidence for such a charge looks like: a criterion recorded before the case was seen, then abandoned. Outside a laboratory that record rarely exists. The second error is to fold this into No true Scotsman or the motte-and-bailey fallacy. Those change the category and the claim; this changes the test, and the three can be run in sequence on the same argument. The third is to read the psychology as validation of the fallacy. Ditto and Lopez's participants were not defending a public position and were never accused of anything, and their asymmetry may be defensible, since an unexpected result is a reason to check the instrument. What makes the finding bite is Study 3, where both diagnoses were made equally unexpected and the asymmetry stayed. The fourth error is the idea that precommitment fixes it. Uhlmann and Cohen's abstract says committing to criteria before seeing the applicant eliminated discrimination; Norton's participants ranked their criteria first and then ignored them; Klein and O'Brien's ten experiments are about people breaking thresholds they had formally set with full information about what might follow. The last error is to confuse the move with hindsight bias, which is about misremembering what one expected rather than about revising what one demands.

Abstract read twice, at Crossref and through NCBI eutils, PMID 15943674. The full text was not obtained: the copy linked from search results at Stanford redirects to a search page, ResearchGate and SAGE return 403, HAL holds a record with no file, and OpenAlex marks the work closed with no repository copy. No sample size for its three studies is therefore quoted here.
